evidence: Each staff member receives a unique user ID. Shared accounts are prohibited. The EHR audit trail records the user ID for each action.
Each staff member receives a unique username for the EHR.
Front desk staff share a login for the scheduling system. Shared logins are permitted at reception.
Our clinic opens at 8 am. Parking is available behind the building.
Every person gets their own credentials; nobody logs in as somebody else, and we can see who changed each chart.
A break-glass account is available during EHR outages. Only the on-call administrator is authorized to enable it. Every use of the break-glass account is logged and reviewed by the security officer.
During a power failure, staff use paper charts until systems return.
Emergency access procedure: the IT manager may grant temporary access in an emergency.
Workstations lock automatically after 15 minutes of inactivity.
The EHR has an idle timeout feature.
Automatic logoff is disabled on the lab workstations.
Our risk assessment found automatic logoff is not reasonable and appropriate for the operating room terminals, which are in a locked room; as an alternative, access to the room is badge-controlled.
All laptops use BitLocker full-disk encryption (AES-256). Recovery keys are stored in the key vault and rotated annually.
Access is role-based and follows least privilege. Managers approve access requests in the ticketing system. Access reviews happen quarterly and accounts are disabled on termination.
Staff can see only the patient data they need for their job.
Anyone on the clinic network can open the shared patient folder.
